Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-2-prompt-long-0041", "row_sha256": "83e4786ca0f5a1f155107d0867a977989d58574a5cb859dae1dc0fd359c5b996", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, could you turn this into a detailed request for a fictional handoff note about a family's photo catalogue? i want one self-contained episode, not a general essay on archiving. the note should sound like something a relative is asking for help with, and it needs to make clear what can be done and what must not be done. the catalogue belongs to the fictional Alvarez family. their photos cover roughly 1980 through 2012, but the material is uneven: there are two labeled albums, several loose prints in a shoebox, and a folder of scanned images on a shared home computer. please use those details, not a different family or a different collection.

some of the album pages have dates written beside them, while other dates are only estimated from the clothes, locations, or people in the pictures. the first album has a handwritten label, “Summer trips,” and includes a 1986 camping weekend near Lake Crescent, though the exact weekend is not recorded. the second is marked “Marta’s school years” and seems to run from 1991 to 1997. don’t turn those clues into more precise dates than they give. the relative who is asking for help remembers that the lake trip was before the family bought its blue station wagon, but doesn’t remember the year they bought it. that can be mentioned as a recollection, not used to calculate a date.

for the loose prints, there are about forty, kept in a shoebox that belonged to Elena. the box has a small card inside with the names “Elena, Luis, Marta” written on it, but it doesn’t say that every photograph contains those people. some photos show birthdays at a house with a green porch; one has a cake with a visible number 8, but the child’s identity isn’t known. a few prints show a beach and a red-striped umbrella, and one has a faded note on the back reading “Cannon Beach?” with the question mark. keep the uncertainty in that note. don’t identify the people in unmarked photos just because their names appear on the card.

the computer folder is called “Family scans” and has 126 image files. it includes scans of some album pages as well as individual pictures, and a handful appear to be duplicates or near-duplicates. the relative has noticed that a scan of a 1994 school concert appears twice, once in color and once in grayscale, but has not checked whether the files are exact copies. the file names include dates and camera-generated numbers, which the family wants to keep intact. do not rename files. that prohibition applies to every file in the folder, including any apparent duplicate; the note should not suggest renaming, even as a way to mark a duplicate. it is fine to sort catalogue entries into year or date groups, and to add a short caption or a note about uncertainty to an entry. make the difference between organizing catalogue information and changing the original file names easy to understand.

there are a few useful details for the handoff note to weave in, but don’t turn them into claims that the whole collection has already been checked. Luis remembers that the school concert was at Marta’s elementary school, probably in spring 1994. Marta thinks it may have been the last concert before the family moved across town, but she is not sure whether the move happened that year or the next. the date in the folder name is 1994-05, and that is the month associated with the scan, not proof of the concert date. the note can say what each clue indicates and keep the family members’ memories attributed to them. it should not resolve their differing recollections or present a guess as confirmed information.

please make the fictional handoff note practical and human, like a relative has started sorting things and wants another family member to continue. it should explain that the next person can review the album labels, enter known dates and captions in the catalogue, and group entries by year where that is supported. they can also make a list of possible duplicates for later review, but the note shouldn’t claim that duplicates have been confirmed or deleted. there is no request to edit the scans, discard prints, or decide who is pictured in uncertain images. keep the request focused on a catalogue handoff, rather than adding a plan for buying equipment, scanning the entire collection, or contacting outside experts.

one numbered section would fit naturally, perhaps a short checklist of what the next relative can do with the catalogue entries. keep it limited to actions already described here, and don’t make it sound like an approved policy for every family. use an ordinary quote somewhere, such as repeating the album label or the little “Cannon Beach?” note, rather than adding a dramatic conversation. give the note connected paragraphs with specific details spread across them; avoid repeating the same prohibition as filler. finish with distinct information: the family hopes to have a small selection of catalogue entries ready to consult before a reunion in October, when they may project three pictures, but nobody has selected those pictures yet. mention that as a reason to make the catalogue easier to browse, not as a decision about which images will be shown.", "output": "Write a detailed, self-contained fictional handoff note about the Alvarez family’s photo catalogue. Make it sound like one relative asking another to continue some practical sorting work, rather than a general essay on archiving. Use the collection details below and distinguish known information from estimates and family recollections. Do not imply that the entire collection has been checked.

The photos cover roughly 1980 through 2012. The collection includes two labeled albums, loose prints in a shoebox, and a folder of scanned images on a shared home computer. The first album is labeled “Summer trips” and includes a 1986 camping weekend near Lake Crescent; the exact weekend is not recorded. The second album is marked “Marta’s school years” and seems to run from 1991 to 1997. A relative remembers that the lake trip happened before the family bought its blue station wagon, but does not remember when they bought it. Attribute this as a recollection and do not use it to infer a more precise date.

The shoebox belonged to Elena and contains about forty loose prints. A card inside lists “Elena, Luis, Marta,” but does not establish that all three appear in every photograph. Some prints show birthdays at a house with a green porch. One shows a cake with the number 8, but the child’s identity is unknown. A few prints show a beach and a red-striped umbrella. One has the faded note “Cannon Beach?” on the back; preserve the question mark and the uncertainty. Do not identify people in unmarked photos based only on the names on the card.

The computer folder is called “Family scans” and contains 126 image files, including scans of album pages and individual pictures. A few files may be duplicates or near-duplicates. A scan of a 1994 school concert appears twice, once in color and once in grayscale, but the relative has not checked whether the files are exact copies. File names include dates and camera-generated numbers. Do not rename files, including any apparent duplicate. You may organize catalogue entries into year or date groups and add a short caption or an uncertainty note to an entry. Make clear that organizing catalogue information does not mean changing original file names.

Include the family’s clues about the school concert without resolving uncertainty. Luis remembers it was at Marta’s elementary school, probably in spring 1994. Marta thinks it may have been the last concert before the family moved across town, but is unsure whether the move happened that year or the next. The folder name includes the date 1994-05; this is the month associated with the scan, not proof of the concert date. Attribute memories to the person who shared them, distinguish them from the folder detail, and do not present a guess as confirmed information.

Make the note practical and human: a relative has begun sorting and wants another family member to continue. Explain that the next person can review album labels, enter known dates and captions in the catalogue, and group entries by year where supported. They may also list possible duplicates for later review, but do not say duplicates have been confirmed or deleted. The request does not include editing scans, discarding prints, or deciding who appears in uncertain images. Keep the handoff focused on catalogue work; do not add plans to buy equipment, scan the entire collection, or contact outside experts.

Include one short numbered checklist of actions the next relative can take, limited to actions described above. Present it as part of this family’s handoff, not as a policy for every family. Use an ordinary quote, such as an album label or the note “Cannon Beach?” Connect the details across paragraphs without repeating the prohibition as filler.

In the final paragraph, mention that the family hopes to have a small selection of catalogue entries ready to consult before a reunion in October. They may project three pictures, but nobody has selected them yet. Present this as a reason to make the catalogue easier to browse, not as a decision about which images will be shown."}]
